t: Minimize the Difference Between Target and Chosen Elements — Fold the Set of Reachable Row-Sums
o: Pick one value from each row so the total lands as close as possible to target. With m, n up to 70 and values up to 70, totals never exceed 70 · 70 = 4900, which makes reachable-sum set DP practical: fold the matrix row by row, extending every achievable partial sum by each value of the incoming row. Example 1 reaches 13 exactly via 1 + 5 + 7, difference 0; Example 2 forces 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 against target 100, difference 94; Example 3 offers 7 nearest to 6 among {1, 2, 7, 8, 9}, difference 1. The final answer is the achievable total minimizing absolute deviation, found by scanning outward from target. Trying all n^m combinations is hopeless at m = 70, while the DP caps work near m · S with S about 4901.
k: Only the SET of achievable partial sums matters — which rows produced a sum is irrelevant, so one boolean layer per row suffices.
The sum ceiling is m times the max value, at most 70 · 70 = 4900; treat that as capacity S for every data structure.
Packing reachable sums into bits turns each row transition into a few shift-and-OR operations — the bitset trick.

a.n: Approach 1: Set / Boolean-Array DP Over Achievable Sums
a.i: Start from the singleton set containing 0. For each row build the next set as every existing partial sum plus every value of the row. Afterwards sweep distance d = 0, 1, 2, ... checking membership of target - d and target + d; the first hit is minimal because candidate totals deviate by whole amounts in either direction. Straightforward and language-neutral.
s: For each row, form next = {s + v} across reachable sums s and row values v.
Replace reachable with next after each row.
Scan d upward and return the first d where target - d or target + d is reachable.
a.t: O(m · S · n) worst case with S = 1 + m · max(mat), fast in practice since the reachable sets saturate early
a.sp: O(S) for the boolean layer or hash set

a.i: Encode the reachable set as bits of one big integer: bit s set means sum s is reachable. Updating for a row is just nxt |= dp << v for each distinct value v, letting the machine process dozens of sum-bits per instruction. Python arbitrary-precision integers make this a few lines, C++ std::bitset likewise, and Java gets a manual word-array version of the same shift-or merge. Same recurrence as Approach 1, divided by the machine word size.
s: Initialize mask = 1, meaning only sum 0 is reachable.
Per row, OR together dp shifted left by each distinct row value; replace dp with the result.
Scan d = 0, 1, 2, ... testing bit target - d and bit target + d; return the first d that hits a set bit.
a.t: O(m · n · S / 64) — each row merge is word-parallel across the sum axis
a.sp: O(S / 64) machine words for the masks

w: Present the sum-set DP first, then offer bit packing as the optimization flourish. Pitfalls: letting sets grow without bound (they naturally cap at S entries here, but say why), checking only one direction when scanning outward from target, and off-by-one errors on the inclusive sum ceiling. Follow-up: recover the actual chosen combination by storing parent pointers per reachable sum, or support negative values, where the reachable window shifts and offset hashing replaces direct indexing.
